conflict_topics: whether to ask the departing colleague to choose an alternative
dialogue_quality_notes: Participants gave concrete, relevant reasons for their positions (halal, coeliac disease, shared grill contamination).
There was a repeated short dispute about whether to ask the departing colleague to pick again; that was resolved by the group assigning themselves the task.
Resolution included a concrete division of labor (D to find nearby place; A to call), which is explicit and actionable.
evaluation.final_reason: By round 11 the group agreed to abandon the original Korean barbecue (incompatible with multiple dietary needs) and to try a nearby Peranakan restaurant, with concrete task assignments to check suitability. Evidence: Turn 22 — Agent D: '...there's a place called PeraMakan... We can call them now to check about the gluten-free options.' Turn 23 — Agent A: 'Good find. I'll call them now and ask about the options.' (Group accepted the alternative and assigned who would check, resolving the dispute about venue and procedure.)
position_change_notes: Agent A initially opposed asking the leaver to pick again (Turn 13: 'I'd rather we didn't put it back on her'), but later advocated asking her (Turn 17: '...Let's just ask her what her second choice would be'). Despite that flip, the group ultimately agreed on an alternative and a plan.
Agent B initially supported the leaver's choice (Turn 2) but quickly accepted changing the venue when dietary issues were raised and preferred not to ask the leaver (Turn 18).
Agent D consistently emphasized dietary/medical constraints, proposed asking the leaver (Turn 12), then volunteered to look up options (Turn 20) and found a nearby alternative (Turn 22).
Agent C consistently noted practical constraints (beef, gluten, proximity) and did not change position; emphasized nearby options (Turn 19).

round_scores.evidence: Turn 3 — Agent C: 'I don't eat beef. Is there other stuff there?' (Raises a dietary incompatibility with the chosen Korean BBQ.)

Turn 4 — Agent D: 'I can't eat there either... I have coeliac disease.' Turn 5 — Agent A: '...I can't eat there either, the meat won't be halal. With Agent D's issue, we definitely need to find another place.' (Multiple substantive dietary restrictions make the chosen venue broadly incompatible.)

Turn 6 — Agent B: 'But she was really looking forward to this place... Can we check if there's anything you can eat?' Turn 7 — Agent C: '...that's three of us who can't eat there. It's not going to work.' (Direct disagreement between keeping the leaver's choice vs switching.)

Turn 8 — Agent B: 'Are there any other ones that might have halal options... we should at least try to find something similar.' Turn 9 — Agent C: '...I don't think that will work for Agent D's coeliac disease. It's probably safer to just pick another type of restaurant.' (Positions move toward finding alternatives rather than insisting on original venue.)

Turn 10 — Agent B: 'Yeah, you're right. That's too much of a risk for Agent D. Okay, so no Korean BBQ then.' Turn 11 — Agent C: '...I have a meeting at 2.30 I can't be late for.' (Agreement to drop the BBQ reduces conflict; scheduling constraint noted.)

Turn 12 — Agent D: 'Should we just ask her what her second choice would be?' Turn 13 — Agent A: 'I'd rather we didn't put it back on her... Can't we find a good alternative and just check if she's happy to go there instead?' (Clear procedural disagreement about whether to ask the leaver.)

Turn 14 — Agent B: 'I agree with Agent A. Let's not make her deal with it. She likes Peranakan food, what about that?' Turn 15 — Agent C: 'That could work.' (Group moves toward an alternative; the procedural dispute is reduced.)

Turn 16 — Agent D: 'A lot of Peranakan dishes use soy sauce. We'd have to check if they can make things gluten-free.' Turn 17 — Agent A: 'You're right. This is getting complicated. Maybe we should just do what you said before, Agent D. Let's just ask her what her second choice would be.' (Agent A reopens the earlier procedural question.)

Turn 18 — Agent B: 'No, let's not ask her. You were right before, Agent A, it'll just make her feel bad. We can figure this out.' Turn 19 — Agent C: 'Find one nearby first.' (Group again pushes to handle selection themselves and to check proximity before calling.)
Turn 20 — Agent D: 'I can look up what's near here.' Turn 21 — Agent A: 'Thanks, Agent D. Let us know what you find.' (Task assignment; no substantive disagreement expressed.)

Turn 22 — Agent D: 'Okay, there's a place called PeraMakan... only a five-minute walk... We can call them now to check about the gluten-free options.' Turn 23 — Agent A: 'Good find. I'll call them now and ask about the options.' (All parties agree on a specific alternative and who will check — concrete mutual plan.)
Turn 24 — Agent D: 'Thanks, Agent A.' (Closure; no new disagreement.)

substantive_insights: Multiple overlapping dietary constraints (halal, avoiding beef, and coeliac disease) made the originally chosen Korean BBQ impractical for the group as a whole.
Tension was not only factual (can they eat there?) but procedural (should they put the burden of re-choosing on the departing colleague?).
A practical compromise — choosing a nearby Peranakan place and checking gluten-free options — reconciled honoring the leaver with accommodating colleagues' dietary needs.

normalizations: Adjusted resolution_round from 11 to 10 to match the conflict trajectory.
